candidates.summary: Spawn founder Jacob Sansbury (@jsnnsa) published an X article on how his 10-person company runs a permanent fleet of AI agents: 77,000 substantial changes shipped in 30 days, $3.1M spent on tokens last month, no pull requests, hourly deploys, and AI 'judges' that answer taste questions from two years of recorded decisions.
facts: Spawn says it is ten people and spends 30x payroll on AI tokens; $3.1 million on tokens last month.
Claims 77,000 substantial changes shipped in the last 30 days, about 108 per hour.
Agents are permanent, named, have memory and real permissions, and each owns an area (engine, finance, bug triage, deploys); they spawn helper agents.
Spawn killed pull requests; agents change code directly, the full test suite runs every 15 minutes, and changes are reviewed by helper agents that did not write them.
Only 1,055 of 123,548 changes were reverted over the last year, about 0.9% (per the article).
An hour without a ship is treated as a SEV-0 incident; rollback of a broken change takes 30 seconds.
AI judges built from recorded decisions returned more than 11,000 verdicts in eight days: 7,296 decided, 2,213 sent back, 1,863 held for a human.
Irreversible actions such as payments go through hard-coded gates.
The author says only Anthropic's Fable model made this work; other labs' models failed in their tests.

source.name: Jacob Sansbury (@jsnnsa) on X: How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World

candidates.summary: A Flamerix AI write-up, at 416 points on Hacker News, says Claude Code sends each background agent's full transcript to its model about every 30 seconds to generate a 3-5 word status line, and measured it at 16.4% of their Claude Code spend in one week. It ships an opt-out preload hook.
facts: Per the gist: every ~30 seconds, for every background agent, Claude Code sends the agent's entire transcript to the agent's model and asks it to describe its most recent action in 3-5 words.

Measured via Claude Code's OpenTelemetry export: agent_summary was 16.4% of Claude Code spend (main conversation 15.7%) and 19.7% of API requests in the week before the hook; 96% of that spend on Opus.
Spend is Claude Code's own per-request cost estimate, not an invoice; on a subscription the loss is rate-limit headroom.
The gist says the behavior is on by default since version 2.1.232 (August 2026) with no setting to turn it off.
It cites GitHub issue anthropics/claude-code#86879 collecting four independent measurements of 18-26%.
The fix is an ~80-line Bun preload loaded via BUN_OPTIONS that suppresses the summary timer; an update can silently undo it.
An HN commenter questioned whether prompt caching makes these calls cheap.

candidates.summary: Matt Pocock shipped a fix to his skills repo after finding that Codex biased most of its subagents to inherit (fork) the parent agent's context window, which hurt skills that need a clean context such as code review and implement-spec.
facts: Pocock: Codex was biasing most of its subagents to inherit its context window from the parent agent, i.e. forking it.
He says this has a big negative impact on skills that rely on a clean context window (code review, implement-spec).
Fix published as mattpocock/skills pull request #1341.

candidates.summary: Starting Oct 30, grandfathered $200 ChatGPT Pro subscribers see Codex and Work usage drop from 20x to 10x the Plus allowance and GPT-6 Pro chat from 200 to 100 messages a week at the same price, per users citing OpenAI's email. Kun Chen argues it pushes coding-heavy users toward Claude.
facts: Multiple X users citing OpenAI's subscriber email: from Oct 30, Codex and Work usage for existing Pro $200 subscribers drops from 20x to 10x the Plus allowance.
Same reports: GPT-6 Pro chat messages drop from 200 to 100 per week; price stays $200/month.
Some posts mention a one-time 62,500-credit grant expiring at year-end as an offset.
Kun Chen speculates OpenAI is conceding consumer coding and focusing on ChatGPT, non-technical work and enterprise API deals.
No primary OpenAI page was read this run; details come from secondhand posts.

related.name: jackcorleone19 on X citing the OpenAI email

candidates.summary: Meta's Alexandr Wang posted that Muse 'just dropped': a personal AI agent at muse.ai that runs tasks on a persistent cloud Linux VM with a browser, works through a mobile and Mac app and WhatsApp, asks approval before sending emails or buying, and uses one-time card numbers at checkout.
facts: muse.ai: 'Muse, AI that gets it done for you': sorts email, books reservations, shops, manages calendars, builds fitness plans.
Every Muse user shares a persistent, isolated Linux computer in the cloud (Muse Secure VM) with a full browser; the user can intervene at any point.
Available in the Muse app on mobile and Mac, or directly in WhatsApp.
Users approve actions such as sending emails and purchases before they happen and get a full audit trail.

Logins go to a credential store Muse can't see (1Password integration 'coming soon'); a one-time card number is generated at checkout, and eligible purchases are covered by Link's purchase protections.
Meta says conversations are not shared with Meta's ad systems; a Muse for Business offering for small businesses is listed.
Page footer: © Meta 2026.
Separately, Artificial Analysis' PersonalityBench ranked Meta's Muse models most 'Friendly' (Muse Spark 1.3 scored 100).

candidates.summary: The Verge reports a bipartisan grassroots backlash against new hyperscale data centers in Arizona over water, as the state faces losing nearly 30% of its Colorado River water while TSMC's fab complex uses nearly 5 million gallons a day.
facts: TSMC's Arizona complex uses nearly 5 million gallons of water a day from Phoenix's municipal supply.
TSMC's projected Arizona spending grew from $12 billion to $265 billion.
Arizona has 172 data centers; newer proposed developments from Phoenix to Tucson face mass, bipartisan opposition.
Some hyperscale data centers, like Google's in The Dalles, Oregon, use about 1.5 million gallons a day.
Arizona will soon lose access to nearly 30% of the water it receives from the Colorado River.

candidates.summary: Ben Thompson interviewed Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar on why the industry under-focuses on AI diffusion, why top-line-focused companies adopt AI better, his frustration that labs don't take a systems-engineering approach to safety, forward-deployed engineering, and Anthropic's fight with the U.S. government.
facts: Stratechery's intro: Sankar thinks the industry is insufficiently focused on AI diffusion.

Topics listed: companies focused on the top line have more success adopting AI; labs' refusal to take a systems engineering approach to AI safety; what Palantir learned from AI; preserving alpha instead of the median; whether more models are needed; what a forward-deployed engineer is; Anthropic vs. the U.S. government.
Full interview is behind the Stratechery subscription; only the free intro was read.

candidates.summary: Emad Mostaque says AI teams no longer need to build good models by hand because the latest AI can do it better, quoting investor Mamoon Hamid's claim that one Mirendil researcher pretrained Mirendil-Base in 3.5 months with agents doing almost all of the engineering.
facts: Mamoon Hamid: one researcher pretrained Mirendil-Base in 3.5 months, with agents doing almost all of the engineering; that researcher now uses Mirendil's product Lor 100% of the time.
Hamid describes Lor as the product Mirendil is building 'to do the work of an entire AI lab'.
Emad Mostaque: 'there is no need for AI teams to build good models any more. Can do it all with latest AI better.'
These are claims from an investor and a commentator; no technical report was read.
